lessons.explanation: The convention is guidance for Claude, not a hard line, and it has to reach every fresh clone with no per-person setup. A CLAUDE.md committed in the repository does that: it is shared through version control, and a file in `engine/` loads when Claude works in that subtree. Putting the rule and a short `Result<T>` example there fixes the six missed pastes for good, and the next six engineers get it with the clone.

a.reasoning: A hook guarantees the result, which is right for a rule that must never be broken. The stem calls a stray `throw` a nuisance that review catches in minutes, so a hook is more than the need. It also adds a pattern scanner to maintain and can block harmless mentions such as comments or tests.

b.reasoning: The setup script automates the wrong layer. The user-level file is personal and is not shared through version control, so the copied text drifts from the wiki when the convention changes and nobody can review it in a pull request.

concept: CLAUDE.md is guidance, not enforced configuration. Use it for conventions Claude should follow, and reserve hooks for rules that must never be broken. Files stack: the user file, the project file and a directory file are all loaded, and nothing is overridden.

Only the project file is shared through version control. The user-level file belongs to one person, so a team convention placed there reaches only those who copy it. A CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory loads on demand, the first time Claude reads, writes or edits a file in that subtree.

c.reasoning: The one-line rule must apply to all code, and a skill loads only when invoked. An engineer who forgets to invoke it gets no card-number rule at all, so the universal standard belongs in CLAUDE.md.
c.tempting: Moving everything into skills removes all 2,500 tokens.

d.reasoning: Editing a committed file by script adds fragile machinery, and the file would differ between branches. A skill gives the same on-demand loading natively.
d.tempting: It keeps both parts in CLAUDE.md and lean for other sessions.

concept: CLAUDE.md loads into every conversation, so it fits project-wide standards and constraints. Use skills for task-specific procedures that are only sometimes relevant.
Project skills in `.claude/skills/` are shared through git. Personal skills in `~/.claude/skills/` are available only to that user.

lessons.explanation: The complaints have two causes: Claude lacks the team's criteria, so it flags allowed patterns, and it has no record of earlier findings, so it repeats them after each push. Documenting the review criteria in CLAUDE.md, including the patterns the team accepts, gives CI-invoked Claude the standards. Including the previous review's findings in the prompt on re-runs lets it report only new or still-open issues.

a.reasoning: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, so a threshold would drop real findings while keeping confident false ones. The problem is missing criteria, not a missing score.
a.tempting: A threshold cuts the volume of comments.

b.reasoning: CLAUDE.md gives CI-invoked Claude the project's review standards. Stating which patterns are allowed removes the false positives at the source.

c.reasoning: Two runs double the cost and time, and both runs still lack the criteria, so both can repeat the same false positives. Agreement between runs does not show a finding is wanted.
c.tempting: Findings that appear twice seem more reliable.

d.reasoning: With earlier findings in the prompt, Claude can skip issues the author already fixed or dismissed. This removes the duplicate comments after each push.

e.reasoning: Batch results can take up to 24 hours, which would hold up a pre-merge check, and it changes nothing about what the review flags. Batching suits work that nothing is waiting on.
e.tempting: Lower cost per run is attractive.

concept: For claude-code-action and CI-invoked Claude Code, put review criteria and project rules in the root CLAUDE.md. Claude follows them when it reviews and responds. Without `--bare`, `-p` loads the same context as an interactive session, including CLAUDE.md.
On re-runs, include prior review findings so Claude reports only new or still-open issues instead of repeating comments.

lessons.explanation: The conventions apply to three paths that are not under one parent, out of about 95 directories. One rule file in `.claude/rules/` with a `paths` list of the three globs loads them only when Claude works with a matching file, in local sessions and in the CI review, with no copies to drift. A parent-directory file would load for every service directory.

a.reasoning: A parent-directory file loads for work in all of `services/`, so about 90 unrelated directories would get the conventions. It also cannot scope `libs/crypto/` correctly. A path-scoped rule covers all three paths exactly.
a.tempting: It covers two of the three directories and can name the third.

b.reasoning: The root file loads in every session, so all engineers carry the 80 lines everywhere. A heading is only a label for Claude, not a condition on loading.
b.tempting: One file with a clear heading keeps the three areas together.

c.reasoning: Three copies must be kept in sync by hand, so they would drift apart. A single file with a glob list gets the same loading with one source of truth.
c.tempting: Each directory's file loads exactly where the work happens.

d.reasoning: One path-scoped rule file lists all three locations, so the conventions load only when Claude works there, in local sessions and in CI. It has no copies, so nothing can drift.

concept: A rule in `.claude/rules/` with `paths:` loads only when Claude works with a matching file. Patterns are relative to the project root, and several globs can sit in one list. A convention that follows a set of separate directories fits one path-scoped rule.
A directory's CLAUDE.md fits one directory tree: it loads when Claude works in that subtree, so a parent-directory file loads for every directory beneath it.

lessons.explanation: Running the reviewer after the merge let defects reach `main`, and 22 needed follow-up fixes. A review that must gate a merge has to run before it. Restoring the reviewer as a blocking pre-merge check, an independent `claude -p` run on the PR diff with criteria in CLAUDE.md, stops the defects, and keeping it on the diff with written criteria keeps the run short.

a.reasoning: Auto-revert cleans up after the defect has already reached `main`, and it can revert good changes on a false positive. The review's timing, not its cleanup, is what needs fixing.
a.tempting: It speeds up merges and still removes bad ones.

b.reasoning: A blocking pre-merge review stops defects before they reach `main`. Limiting it to the diff with written criteria keeps the run short, and an independent instance keeps it unbiased.

c.reasoning: Batch fits work nothing waits on, such as a nightly audit, and results can take up to 24 hours. A nightly run finds defects a day after merge, so the 22 follow-up fixes would continue.
c.tempting: Batch is cheaper than a synchronous run.

d.reasoning: The author's session is less effective at spotting its own mistakes because it carries the reasoning behind them. Removing the independent job saves the 4 minutes but loses the reviewer's value.
d.tempting: No new job is needed and the author already has the context.

concept: Code Review as a managed service never approves or blocks a PR, so a merge gate needs a check that runs before the merge. The Message Batches API processes requests asynchronously, with results available later up to 24 hours, so a blocking check cannot use it.
The session that wrote a change is not the best judge of it. Review from a clean context with the diff and written criteria.

stemSignals.phrase: moved it to run on `main` after the merge
stemSignals.meaning: Defects now arrive after the merge.

stemSignals.phrase: 22 merged PRs needed follow-up fixes
stemSignals.meaning: The cost of reviewing too late.

stemSignals.phrase: two of them touched card-handling services
stemSignals.meaning: The risk is in what reaches `main`.

stemSignals.phrase: cut the 4 minutes, but not at the price of defects reaching `main`
stemSignals.meaning: The check must stay before the merge.

lookFor: A blocking check that runs before the merge.
An independent instance on the diff with written criteria.
No asynchronous batch or after-the-fact cleanup.

eliminate.reason: It reacts after the defect has reached `main` and can revert good changes.
A nightly batch finds defects after merge, so the follow-up fixes continue.
The author's session carries its own reasoning, so it misses its own mistakes.

lessons.rule: A review that must gate a merge runs synchronously and independently before the merge. Batch review suits only work nothing waits on.

lessons.explanation: The prose spec was read two ways, so the results vary. Two or three concrete input and output examples, such as `0.125 -> 0.12` and `0.135 -> 0.14`, show the exact tie-breaking rule that includes a half rounding down and a half rounding up. Claude can then match every one, and the examples can double as tests.

a.reasoning: More prose is the same kind of input that was already interpreted two ways. Concrete examples show the tie-breaking rule directly and leave much less room for reading it differently.
a.tempting: A fuller explanation of the ledger's rule seems to remove the doubt.

b.reasoning: Examples that include several halves show the exact tie-breaking rule, so Claude can infer it instead of guessing. Two or three varied cases are enough, and they can double as tests.

c.reasoning: Sampling temperature is an API parameter; Claude Code has no session temperature setting. Even where one exists, it would only make runs alike and not choose the ledger's rule.
c.tempting: Consistent runs seem to be the actual goal.

d.reasoning: A single example fits several rules, such as always rounding halves down, and it says nothing about `0.135`. Varied examples that include a half going up pin the rule down.
d.tempting: One example is a concrete reference.

concept: Examples, one-shot or multi-shot, show instead of tell. They are especially useful for corner cases and exact output formats, and several examples are needed when there are several edge cases. The exam guide recommends 2 to 3 concrete input and output examples when prose is read inconsistently.
Sampling temperature is an API parameter; Claude Code has no session temperature setting.

Examples that can serve as tests.
